question.question:
A company pays dividends every quarter; the one just paid was 0.65 USD per share. Stage one covers 11 quarters, during which every quarterly dividend exceeds the preceding one by -125 basis points (a basis point is 0.01 percent; a negative figure means a cut), so the quarter-1 dividend already reflects one quarter of growth. Once stage one ends, dividends rise at 1 percent a year in perpetuity, turned into a quarterly growth rate by the nominal convention: 'compound' uses the rate that, compounded across four quarters, yields the annual rate, and 'nominal' divides the annual percentage by four. Investors require an effective annual return of 5.5 percent; translate it into the equivalent compounded quarterly rate and discount every quarterly dividend at that rate. The terminal value at the close of the final stage-one quarter is the first stage-two dividend divided by the quarterly rate minus the quarterly stage-two growth; no valuation exists unless that growth is lower than the quarterly rate. Give the quarterly discount rate in percent, the present value of the stage-one dividends, the terminal value at the end of stage one, and today's share price (stage-one present value plus discounted terminal value).

Answer format: use exact arithmetic through all intermediate steps, round only the final value half up to 2 decimal digits, and return only the numeric value interpreted in `usd` with no unit label or additional text.

Present value today of all stage-one quarterly dividends per share
